newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC fudge gives good nudge to WTO, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: APEC fudge gives good nudge to WTO, analysts say.

text.p: The annual APEC conference produced agreements that were fudged enough to let all sides claim success but will give good impetus for next month's inaugural World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore, analysts said on Tuesday.

The biggest triumph in everybody's-a-winner trade diplomacy at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit was an artful dodge over a U.S.-backed plan to have free trade in the trillion-dollar information technology business by the turn of the century.
A statement following the summit on Monday called on the WTO "to substantially eliminate tariffs by the year 2000". But it "recognised the need for flexibility".
"Substantially eliminate is tradespeak for zero," said U.S. Trade Repesentative Jay Ziegler.

But Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, who will host December's WTO meeting, said that while the statement was helpful "it will not lead to a firm conclusion that we are going to free up the information sector by the year 2000.
"It (the leaders' statement) could be treated by members any way they want to," Goh said.
That was also the interpretation of Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad. "If we feel we are not ready then we don't have to meet the deadline," he told reporters.
"It was a fudge, but it was a positive fudge," Desmond Supple, an economist at IDEA research house in Singapore, told Reuters.
Still, the adoption of the paragraph on ITA "is a sign that we could get some fairly good progress at the WTO meeting in Singapore," Supple said.
The biggest boost for the WTO at this summit was a possible breakthrough on China's admission to the body.

China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said Beijing expects to conclude its talks with the United States over its admission in the first half of next year -- before U.S. President Bill Clinton and China's President Jiang Zemin exchange the visits they announced at this summit.
U.S. insistence that China join the WTO as a developed member rather than on the easier terms available to under-developed nations is one of the main obstacles to Beijing's membership.

"APEC plays a very useful role because it serves as a challenge to WTO," said George Manzano, research director at University of Asia and Pacific in Manila. "If APEC can do it on a voluntary basis, the WTO should be able to do the same."

Other economists in the region were less than impressed with the initial offerings of the 18 countries in working towards the world's biggest free trade and investment area over the next quarter-century. Each country put forward its first steps toward dismantling trade barriers under the Manila Action Plan.
"They were talking about the very distant future," said K.K. Chan, chief economist at Nomura Research Institute in Tokyo.
Liew Yin Sze, an economist with J.M. Sassoon in Singapore, agreed. "The free trade issue is nothing new. Everybody seems to be working towards it, even without APEC."

But Raul Ruiz, vice-president for research at Sun Hung Kai Securities, said consumers will benefit in the long run from the lower prices that come with lower tariffs and exporters will benefit from expanding markets.
The leaders hoped their efforts would bear fruit at the WTO.
"We call on WTO members to build on the process of progressive liberalisation and enhanced transparency that we have initiated in APEC," their statement said.

The next big battleground is likely to be over transparency at WTO. Japan and the United States are pushing for an agreement calling for more transparency in government contracts and tenders, and criminalisation of bribery.
It would also call for "national treatment" for foreign investors, allowing them to have 100 percent equity in foreign ventures.
The APEC leaders' statement did not mention the subject, but a separate declaration by their foreign and trade ministers did.
